summary: Earthbox is an interactive terminal-based sonification workstation that turns NASA satellite imagery and scientific visualizations into sound. Built in Go, it fetches public-domain frames from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio and Earth Information Center, then analyzes each image’s luminance, color, pixel density, edge motion, and spatial distribution to drive pitch, instrumentation, tempo, and stereo panning. This creates an auditory alternative to visual charts, making satellite observation data accessible to visually impaired users and engaging for students and the public. Because it runs entirely inside a standard terminal with no heavy setup, it is a lightweight educational tool for science outreach and storytelling.
details:
Earthbox works by decoding a NASA frame and extracting four core visual properties. Luminance and brightness set the root frequency and harmonic lift. Color dominance and warmth select the synthesizer instrument profile and timbre. Pixel density and edge motion control note density, tempo, and pacing. Spatial luminance distribution governs stereo panning and field width. Users can switch between Scientific, Cinematic, Accessible, and Chaos listening modes, adjust a fidelity slider that blends raw data mappings with musical harmony, and view real-time ANSI true-color renderings, spectrum analyzers, and waveform displays.

The project is built in Go for concurrency, memory efficiency, and deterministic binaries. The interface uses the Charmbracelet ecosystem (bubbletea, lipgloss, bubbles) for responsive layouts and key-driven control. The audio engine uses pre-allocated PCM buffers to avoid per-sample allocation overhead and generates 16-bit 44.1 kHz WAV output with concurrent caching. FFmpeg handles frame extraction and stream processing, and native OS audio subprocesses (afplay on macOS, ffplay on Linux and Windows) handle playback.

Earthbox benefits accessibility by offering sound-based access to satellite data, supports education as a zero-dependency tool that runs in any modern terminal, and supports storytelling through “Earth Stories” and NASA attribution for every dataset. A one-key exporter bundles the WAV audio, raw NASA frame, structured JSON mappings, and scientific documentation into a shareable .earthbox package.

The main design challenge was balancing scientific accuracy with listenability. Raw one-to-one mappings can produce harsh noise, while overly musical interpretations can hide the data. The adjustable fidelity matrix lets users move between strict translations and harmonically supported soundscapes. Performance was also a priority, with adjacent preset prefetching, URL-hash caching, and sub-millisecond synthesis ensuring immediate responsiveness and no playback lag.
